implementation_notes: System.Text.Json ships with the runtime: JsonSerializer.Serialize/Deserialize<T> (or a source-generated JsonSerializerContext) is the serializer and an EF Core ValueConverter<Graph, string> registers the column, so no hand-written mapper survives. Polymorphic graphs need JsonDerivedType attributes, and because the graph is one converted value the context cannot see changes inside it unless the property is replaced.
pitfalls: EF Core compares the converted value with Equals to detect changes, so a graph type without value equality marks the entity dirty on every save while in-place mutations inside a reference-typed property stay invisible.
BinaryFormatter and the legacy [Serializable] path are blocked or removed for security reasons in modern .NET; do not reintroduce them as the persistence format.
Trimmed or AOT-published builds need a JsonSerializerContext, since reflection-based serialization breaks or warns at publish time.

variants.name: EF Core 8 mapped JSON column (ToJson)
variants.implementation_notes: EF Core 8 maps an owned entity or complex type to a real JSON column with ToJson(), so the database stores the graph as JSON text while the model stays an ordinary object graph and LINQ can translate queries into the document on supported providers. Choose it when the store is SQL Server/Azure SQL, PostgreSQL or SQLite and the payload should stay queryable; it trades full opacity for provider-specific query support.
pitfalls: JSON column mapping needs EF Core 8+ and a capable provider; on older stacks the mapping silently degrades to a string column without query translation.
Updating a nested element rewrites the whole JSON column, so high-churn nested writes amplify and can conflict across writers.
